home-remodeling.title: Home Remodeling in Miami's Upper East Side | PGX Builders
home-remodeling.meta_description: Whole-home remodeling in Miami's Upper East Side — Morningside, Belle Meade, Bay Point. Licensed GC, HEPB-fluent, 100% permitted. Call (786) 273-2524.
home-remodeling.h1: Remodeling the Upper East Side's originals
home-remodeling.hero_sub: Licensed, permitted whole-home remodeling for the Upper East Side's 1920s-to-1950s houses — from HEPB approvals in Morningside to full structural and systems work, supervised daily by PGX Builders Group.
home-remodeling.local_heading: The neighborhoods that kept their architecture
intro_paragraphs: Miami's Upper East Side kept the houses other neighborhoods tore down. Morningside's 1920s Mediterranean Revival and Art Deco homes sit on wide, canopied streets; Belle Meade holds Streamline Moderne and vernacular houses from the 1920s through the 1940s behind its single guard gate; Bay Point's estates stretch to the bay. Owners here rarely want a teardown — they want a full remodel that keeps the facade, the proportions, and the character, and replaces nearly everything behind them: layout, plumbing, electrical, roof structure, windows, finishes.

The City of Miami Building Department issues the permits here, and that is only the first gate. Morningside was the city's first locally designated historic district, and Bayside and Palm Grove carry the same protection — exterior changes there need a Certificate of Appropriateness, reviewed at staff level or by the Historic and Environmental Preservation Board. On bayfront streets in FEMA flood zones, substantial-improvement rules can shape how far a remodel goes. We map all of it before you sign anything, so the approvals path is part of the plan, not a surprise in month three.

PGX Builders Group has spent 20-plus years remodeling South Florida homes, and older houses are where that experience earns its keep. You get a fixed written scope, a licensed general contractor (CGC1539072), and a supervisor on site every working day — someone who knows what 1930s masonry does when you open it up. We protect original floors and plaster while the structure is exposed, coordinate gate access in Belle Meade and Bay Point without drama, and keep one accountable team on the job from the first estimate through the warranty.

faqs.q: Do I need historic approval to remodel a house in Morningside?
faqs.a: For interior work, no — historic designation governs what the public can see. For exterior changes such as windows, doors, additions, and even exterior paint on contributing homes, you need a Certificate of Appropriateness. Straightforward, like-for-like changes are often approved at staff level; larger ones go to the Historic and Environmental Preservation Board. We prepare the application materials and manage the review, because that beats repairing a stop-work order.

faqs.q: How long do City of Miami permits take for a whole-home remodel?
faqs.a: It depends on scope. A remodel with structural changes needs engineered drawings and multiple plan reviewers, and historic-district projects add the Certificate of Appropriateness step in front. Realistically, think in months rather than weeks for approvals on a full renovation — and we use that window for cabinetry lead times and material selections so the schedule overlaps instead of stacking. We handle submittals and revisions ourselves rather than leaving you to chase reviewers.

faqs.q: We're on the water — does the FEMA 50% rule affect our remodel?
faqs.a: Possibly, and it's better to know before you fall in love with a scope. In mapped flood zones, when the cost of improvements exceeds half the building's market value, the entire structure can be required to meet current flood elevation standards. Bayfront streets in Morningside, Belle Meade, and Shorecrest sit in flood-prone territory, so we run that math with you at the estimate stage and shape the scope around the answer.

faqs.q: What does it cost to renovate a whole Upper East Side house?
faqs.a: A wide range, honestly — the spread between refreshing finishes and gutting a 1935 house to its shell is enormous, and structural work, historic approvals, and finish level move the number more than square footage does. We're a high-end contractor and rarely the lowest bid; what you get instead is a fixed written scope, daily supervision, and a number that means something. We'll give you a real figure after a walk-through.

faqs.q: Can we live in the house during a full remodel?
faqs.a: During a true whole-home remodel we advise against it — you'd be sharing the house with demolition, re-piping, and open ceilings, and projects run slower and costlier when crews work around a family. For phased remodels we can wall off zones with real dust containment and keep one bathroom and a working kitchen alive. We'll tell you honestly which kind of project yours is before contract.

home-remodeling.cta_sub: Walk us through the house, tell us how you want to live in it, and get a written scope — in English o en español.

kitchen-remodeling.title: Kitchen Remodeling for Miami's Upper East Side | PGX Builders
kitchen-remodeling.meta_description: Custom kitchens for 1920s-50s Upper East Side homes. Cabinetry, stone, gas, lighting — permitted through the City of Miami. Free estimate: (786) 273-2524.
kitchen-remodeling.hero_sub: Custom kitchens for houses that predate the modern kitchen — cabinetry, stone, gas, and lighting built and permitted by a licensed Miami general contractor, with a PGX supervisor on site daily.
intro_paragraphs: The original kitchens in Morningside, Palm Grove, and Belle Meade were designed to be hidden — small, closed rooms at the back of the house, built when nobody entertained in them. Today the kitchen is where these Upper East Side homes live, so owners open them to the dining room, add an island in honed stone, and commission cabinetry that holds its own next to ninety-year-old plaster and hardwood. Done well, a new kitchen feels inevitable in a 1938 house. Done poorly, it looks like a showroom crashed into it. We build the first kind.

A kitchen remodel here is a City of Miami permit job — building, electrical, plumbing, and mechanical — and in these houses it usually uncovers the original infrastructure: cloth-insulated wiring, galvanized supply lines, undersized panels. Removing the wall between kitchen and dining room means engineering, because most of these walls are load-bearing masonry. And if your street is inside the Morningside, Bayside, or Palm Grove historic district, any exterior change — a new window over the sink, a relocated vent — needs a Certificate of Appropriateness before it needs a permit. We handle both, in the right order.

Every PGX kitchen begins as a fixed written scope, allowances spelled out rather than discovered along the way. Our supervisor is on site daily, the cabinetry is measured after the walls are straightened rather than before, and the stone templating happens once the boxes are set — the sequence that separates a tight kitchen from an expensive one with gaps. With 150-plus remodels and additions delivered across South Florida, we have made peace with old houses. They still surprise us; they no longer surprise our budgets.

scope_items.desc: Shop-built boxes and fronts to your designer's or our drawings, scribed to plaster walls that have not been square since 1940.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a kitchen remodel in Miami?
faqs.a: Yes. Anything beyond paint and swapping appliances in place — new circuits, moved plumbing, removed walls, relocated gas — requires City of Miami permits and inspections. Unpermitted kitchen work surfaces at the worst possible time: appraisal, insurance renewal, or closing. PGX permits every job, which is exactly what you want to be able to say when you eventually sell a house in this neighborhood.

faqs.q: Will historic district rules affect an interior kitchen remodel?
faqs.a: Usually not — the Morningside, Bayside, and Palm Grove designations govern exterior appearance, and a kitchen that stays inside the existing walls is reviewed like any other permit. The exceptions are changes visible from outside: a new or enlarged window, a relocated exterior door, a vent through a street-facing facade. Those need a Certificate of Appropriateness first, and we build that step into the schedule when it applies.

faqs.q: Can you open the kitchen to the dining room in an older masonry house?
faqs.a: Almost always, with engineering. Most interior walls in these 1920s-to-1940s houses are load-bearing masonry, so the opening gets a properly sized beam, shoring during the work, and city inspections — not a saw and confidence. It is the single most transformative move available in these floor plans, and it is the kind of structural work we do week in, week out.

faqs.q: How long does a custom kitchen take?
faqs.a: Construction itself typically runs a few months; the honest schedule driver is lead time — custom cabinetry and slab selection can take longer than the building work, and appliance deliveries have opinions of their own. We sequence ordering during permitting so the waiting overlaps, and we never demolish your kitchen until the long-lead items are confirmed. You get a schedule in writing and a supervisor who keeps it.

faqs.q: What does a high-end kitchen cost in this area?
faqs.a: It varies widely with cabinetry, stone, appliances, and how much structure and infrastructure the project touches — in these houses, panel upgrades and re-piping often ride along. We would rather scope your actual kitchen than quote a fantasy average. Expect a serious investment, expect it itemized line by line in writing, and expect the final number to match the contract. That last part is the one that matters.

kitchen-remodeling.cta_sub: Show us the kitchen you have and describe the one you want — we'll answer with a written scope, in English o en español.

bathroom-remodeling.title: Miami Upper East Side Bathroom Remodeling | PGX Builders
bathroom-remodeling.meta_description: Primary baths and full gut bathroom remodels across Miami's Upper East Side. Waterproofing done right in 90-year-old houses. Call PGX at (786) 273-2524.
bathroom-remodeling.hero_sub: Primary suites, frameless showers, and stone baths for the Upper East Side's older homes — fully permitted through the City of Miami, waterproofed correctly, and supervised daily by a licensed contractor.
intro_paragraphs: The bathrooms that came with the Upper East Side's houses — in Morningside, Bayside, and Shorecrest alike — were an afterthought: one per floor, tiled in pastel, sized for people in a hurry. The remodel most owners want now is a true primary suite, with a bedroom or oversized closet converted into a bath holding a freestanding tub, a frameless shower, book-matched stone, and lighting that flatters rather than interrogates. In a 1930s house that transformation is as much plumbing strategy as design, and it rewards a contractor who has opened up these floors before.

Every bathroom remodel here is permitted through the City of Miami Building Department, with plumbing, electrical, and building inspections included. What the permit card doesn't show is what we find under it: original cast-iron drain lines near the end of their service life, galvanized supply pipes ready for retirement, framing that has hosted a leak or two since the Kennedy administration. We scope the house's plumbing honestly before we quote, because replacing a corroded stack mid-project is exactly the surprise a fixed contract exists to prevent. Interior work rarely involves historic review; changing exterior windows in a designated district does.

Waterproofing is where bathroom budgets go to be vindicated or embarrassed, usually years later. PGX installs full membrane systems behind every shower and flood-tests pans before a single tile goes down — details nobody photographs and nobody should ever have to think about again. Add daily site supervision, dust containment that respects the rest of an occupied home, and a written scope that names your fixtures and stone before demolition starts, and you get the version of a bathroom remodel that ends with everyone still on speaking terms.

faqs.q: Can you add a primary bathroom to a 1930s Upper East Side house?
faqs.a: Yes — it is our most requested project in Morningside and Bayside. The design question is where the plumbing can run: these houses sit on slabs or shallow floor structures, so drain routing gets planned before anything is promised. A bedroom or generous closet usually donates the space. We handle the engineering, the City of Miami permits, and the reality that no two of these houses were built quite alike.

faqs.q: Do bathroom remodels need permits in the City of Miami?
faqs.a: Yes — moving fixtures, altering plumbing or electrical, or changing walls all require permits and inspections. A tile-and-vanity refresh with everything staying in place is lighter, but most remodels worth doing here go further than that. Permitted work protects you at resale and keeps your insurer friendly. We pull every permit and meet every inspector; it is in the contract, not an upsell.

faqs.q: The house is on a slab — can the shower or drain move?
faqs.a: Yes. We saw-cut the slab, re-route the drain lines, and pour back — routine work when it is planned, miserable when it is improvised. In houses of this age we also scope the existing cast-iron lines while the slab is open, because that is the cheapest moment you will ever have to replace them. It adds a line to the scope and subtracts a future emergency.

faqs.q: Will the historic district care about my bathroom remodel?
faqs.a: Interior bathroom work does not go through historic review, even in Morningside or Palm Grove. It only enters the picture if the project changes the exterior — enlarging a window for the new shower wall, say, or adding a vent visible from the street. If your design touches the facade, we prepare the Certificate of Appropriateness paperwork; if it doesn't, the district won't slow you down at all.

faqs.q: Why is waterproofing such a big deal in Miami bathrooms?
faqs.a: Humidity, hard use, and — in this neighborhood — old structures that have already survived one era of leaks. Behind our showers goes a full membrane system, sloped and flood-tested before tile; around the room goes ventilation sized for actual South Florida moisture. None of it shows in photographs, and all of it decides whether the bathroom still looks new in a decade. We consider that the point.

home-additions.title: Home Additions in Morningside & the Upper East Side, Miami
home-additions.meta_description: Home additions in Miami's Upper East Side — rear extensions, second stories, HEPB review handled. City of Miami permits included. Call (786) 273-2524.
home-additions.hero_sub: Rear extensions, second stories, and new primary wings for Upper East Side homes — engineered, permitted through the City of Miami, cleared through historic review where required, and built under daily supervision.
intro_paragraphs: The Upper East Side has generous lots and, by today's standards, modest houses. A 1930s Morningside home often offers less space than its lot could gracefully carry — which is why rear extensions, primary-suite wings, and carefully judged second stories are how families stay in Belle Meade, Palm Grove, and Bayside instead of leaving them. The best additions here read as if the original architect returned with a bigger budget: same proportions, same materials, more house. That standard is the job.

An addition is where this area's rulebook earns respect. Inside the Morningside, Bayside, and Palm Grove historic districts, new construction needs a Certificate of Appropriateness from the City of Miami's Historic and Environmental Preservation Board — rear-facing additions that defer to the original street elevation have the smoothest path. Everywhere in the neighborhood, permits and inspections run through the City of Miami Building Department under Miami 21 zoning. And on bayfront lots in FEMA flood zones, we do the substantial-improvement math early, because it can decide how ambitious the project should be.

Structurally, additions in this neighborhood are marriages of 1930s masonry and current Florida Building Code — new foundations tied to old footings, tie beams and hurricane strapping the original builders never imagined, stucco profiles matched so the seam disappears. PGX has delivered 150-plus remodels and additions across South Florida, every one permitted and inspected. You get one contract, one accountable team, a supervisor on site daily, and — in Belle Meade and Bay Point — crews that treat the gate, the neighbors, and the schedule with equal care.

faqs.q: Can I add a second story in the Morningside historic district?
faqs.a: Sometimes — it depends on the house and the design. The Historic and Environmental Preservation Board reviews additions for compatibility, and second stories that overwhelm a contributing home's street presence get pushed back. Set-back upper floors and rear-facing massing have a far better record. We tell you early and honestly whether your concept is likely to pass review, because designing around the answer is cheaper than arguing with it.

faqs.q: How does the FEMA substantial-improvement rule affect additions here?
faqs.a: On lots in mapped flood zones — much of the bayfront in this neighborhood — if the value of the work crosses half the building's market value, current flood elevation requirements can apply to the whole structure. That can reshape a project or occasionally argue for a different one. We run this analysis during estimating, in writing, so the decision gets made at the kitchen table instead of at plan review.

faqs.q: Is building inside Belle Meade's gate complicated?
faqs.a: Less than people fear. Permits are still City of Miami — the gate changes logistics, not jurisdiction. We schedule deliveries tightly, keep the street clean, and make sure crews going in and out are expected, because a contractor's reputation inside a gated neighborhood is built one workday at a time. Neighbors talk on these streets. We would rather they talk about how quiet the job was.

faqs.q: How long does a home addition take from design to done?
faqs.a: Plan on a real timeline: design and engineering first, then historic review where it applies, then City of Miami permitting, then construction — several months at minimum, and longer for second stories or bayfront lots. What we control is honesty about the schedule and daily supervision once we are building. What kills addition timelines is usually the gap between phases, so we manage all of them under one roof.

faqs.q: Will the addition match the original house?
faqs.a: That is the craft. We match stucco textures, roof slopes, eave details, and window proportions so the addition reads as family, not a guest. In the historic districts, review standards actually ask new work to be subtly distinguishable from old — compatible, not counterfeit — and a good design does both. Either way, the goal is that in five years nobody remembers where the house used to end.

outdoor-living.title: Outdoor Living, Upper East Side Miami FL | PGX Builders
outdoor-living.meta_description: Terraces, summer kitchens, driveways and impact openings for Upper East Side homes near Biscayne Bay. Licensed Miami GC — call PGX at (786) 273-2524.
outdoor-living.hero_sub: Terraces, summer kitchens, pergolas, driveways, and impact openings for Upper East Side homes — built for salt air, engineered for the wind zone, permitted through the City of Miami, and supervised daily.
outdoor-living.local_heading: Between the Boulevard and the bay
intro_paragraphs: East of Biscayne Boulevard, the yards end at the water — Belle Meade Island, the eastern streets of Morningside, the waterfront edge of Shorecrest — and even the inland blocks live under a tree canopy that makes outdoor rooms the point of the whole neighborhood. Upper East Side owners invest in covered terraces, summer kitchens with real gas and real ventilation, pergolas built to engineering rather than optimism, and driveways and facades that finally match what happened inside the house. Miami weather is generous; salt air is not. We design for both.

Exterior work here is permitted through the City of Miami, and anything visible from the street inside the Morningside, Bayside, or Palm Grove historic districts — fences, driveways, front terraces, even exterior paint on contributing houses — goes through a Certificate of Appropriateness first. Impact windows, doors, and roofing must carry Miami-Dade product approvals for the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone. And because parts of this neighborhood know street flooding personally, we treat drainage as scope rather than afterthought: grading, drains, and hardscape that sheds water away from the house instead of toward it.

PGX builds exteriors with the materials this climate demands — marine-grade hardware, stainless fasteners, stone and stucco systems specified for salt exposure — and sequences the work so trades don't undo each other: re-roof before the new terrace ceiling, impact openings before the final stucco and paint. One licensed, insured contractor (CGC1539072) carries the whole scope in writing, one supervisor walks the site daily, and the crews leave gated streets the way they found them. It is exterior work run like interior work, which is rarer than it should be.

scope_items.desc: Miami-Dade approved windows, doors, and roofing coordinated in the right order, so warranties and inspections all land cleanly.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a pergola or summer kitchen in Miami?
faqs.a: Almost always. Anything with footings, a roof, gas, water, or electricity is permitted work in the City of Miami, and in a High-Velocity Hurricane Zone the structure needs engineering and approved products regardless of size. A summer kitchen adds gas and plumbing inspections to the list. It is paperwork we do constantly, and it is what separates an asset from a liability when the house sells.

faqs.q: Can I change my driveway or fence in the historic district?
faqs.a: Yes, with a Certificate of Appropriateness — in Morningside, Bayside, and Palm Grove, work visible from the street goes through the City of Miami's historic preservation review before permitting. Materials and design matter, since the review favors choices in character with the district. We prepare the application and handle the process; most well-designed driveway and fence proposals move through without drama.

faqs.q: What outdoor materials actually survive this close to the bay?
faqs.a: Salt air is patient and undefeated, so we specify for it: stainless or marine-grade hardware, powder-coated aluminum or true exterior hardwoods, stone sealed for the exposure, stucco detailed to shed water. Cheap fasteners are where bayfront pergolas go to die. The right material list costs more on day one and dramatically less by year five — that trade is the entire philosophy of exterior work here.

faqs.q: Our street floods in heavy rain — can outdoor work help?
faqs.a: It can help your lot, which is the part you control. Sections of the Upper East Side, Shorecrest especially, see street flooding during king tides and hard storms, so we grade terraces and driveways to move water away from the structure and add drains where they earn their keep. We won't promise to fix the street — nobody honest will — but your slab and finishes shouldn't pay for the city's stormwater schedule.

faqs.q: Can you coordinate a re-roof with the rest of the exterior work?
faqs.a: Yes, and you want it coordinated: roof first, then terrace ceilings and paint, with impact openings sequenced so flashing and stucco tie in correctly. Every product goes in with Miami-Dade approvals and the inspections to match. One contract and one supervisor means no gap between trades where warranties go to hide. That coordination is most of what people are actually buying from a general contractor.

outdoor-living.cta_sub: Invite us to see the yard, the roof, and the plan in your head — estimates in English o en español.

permitting-compliance.title: Upper East Side Permits & Compliance, Miami | PGX Builders
permitting-compliance.meta_description: Permit filings, HVHZ approvals, inspections and open-permit closeouts for Morningside, Belle Meade and Shorecrest homes. Licensed GC. Call (786) 273-2524.
permitting-compliance.h1: The open permit nobody told you about
permitting-compliance.hero_sub: We pull City of Miami permits for Upper East Side houses, meet the inspectors, and close the file — including the expired one a prior owner left behind. Licensed general contractor, CGC1539072, supervising every job daily.
intro_paragraphs: Houses in Miami's Upper East Side have been changing hands, and changing shape, since the 1920s. A Mediterranean Revival on a Morningside street, a Streamline Moderne behind Belle Meade's gate, a 1940s house in Palm Grove or Magnolia Park, a bayfront property in Shorecrest — most carry a permit history several owners deep, and somewhere in it sits a job that was never signed off. A roof, a window swap, a pool enclosure, a garage quietly turned into a guest room. None of it announces itself until a title search finds it, weeks before a closing or a refinance.

Work here is filed with the City of Miami Building Department, through the city's iBuild and ePlan systems under Miami 21 zoning — the first gate, not the only one. Morningside, Bayside and Palm Grove are locally designated historic districts, and the MiMo Biscayne Boulevard district runs along the corridor, so exterior changes there need a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Historic and Environmental Preservation Board. Windows, doors and roof assemblies need Miami-Dade product approvals for the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone. Bayfront lots add flood-zone review, and the apartment and condominium buildings around Shorecrest carry recertification and milestone obligations of their own.

PGX Builders Group is a licensed general contractor rather than a permit runner, and that distinction shows when a file has to be closed instead of merely opened. We begin by reading what the city and the county already hold on the property, then tell you plainly what is outstanding, how much of it is paperwork and how much is real work. Where the file needs an architect, a structural engineer or a surveyor, we engage and coordinate them. Scope is written before anything begins, a supervisor meets every inspector on site, and one team carries it from application to final approval.

faqs.q: A title search on our Morningside house found an open permit. What now?
faqs.a: An open or expired permit follows the property, not the contractor who pulled it, and a title company will hold your closing until it clears. We start with the record: what was permitted, what was actually built, what is still missing. If the original contractor has disappeared, we can become the contractor of record and obtain permission to complete the work. Concealed work sometimes needs an engineer's letter. Then inspections, then the final. Plan on weeks rather than days, and start long before the closing date.

faqs.q: Who issues building permits for the Upper East Side?
faqs.a: The City of Miami Building Department. Unlike Miami Shores Village next door, the Upper East Side is not its own municipality — Morningside, Belle Meade, Bay Point, Bayside, Palm Grove, Shorecrest and Magnolia Park all file with the city, applications through iBuild and drawings through ePlan, under Miami 21 zoning. Behind the city sits Miami-Dade County, whose product control approvals govern anything installed in the High-Velocity Hurricane Zone and whose recertification program reaches buildings once they hit a certain age.

faqs.q: Does historic designation change the permit process in Morningside?
faqs.a: Only for what the street can see. Interior work is reviewed like any other permit. Exterior changes in Morningside, Bayside and Palm Grove — windows, doors, roofing, fences, additions, even paint on a contributing house — need a Certificate of Appropriateness before a building permit can issue. Modest, like-for-like changes are often handled at staff level; larger ones go to the Historic and Environmental Preservation Board. We prepare the application and carry it through, with that step built into the schedule instead of discovered halfway.

faqs.q: The previous owner closed in the garage without a permit. Can that be legalized?
faqs.a: Often, yes, and it is far better to do it before the house goes on the market. The path runs backwards: an architect or engineer documents what exists, we open finishes so an inspector can see the wiring, framing and plumbing now hidden behind them, and the space is brought up to current code — egress, smoke alarms, HVHZ openings. Then it is permitted and inspected as built. Occasionally zoning will not allow the use at all, and the honest answer is to restore the space.

faqs.q: Our building near Shorecrest received a recertification notice. Do you handle the repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. The inspection itself is an engineer's or architect's job, and we bring one in rather than claim it as ours. Our part is what the report demands: concrete and stucco restoration, waterproofing, balconies and railings, electrical corrections, plus the permits and inspections that close the file. Miami-Dade recertification reaches buildings by age and repeats on a cycle after that; the state milestone inspection applies to condominium and cooperative buildings three habitable stories and taller, with the structural integrity reserve study alongside it. We price the repair scope in writing.
